name: Wei Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wei. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything today is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No worries. I run a loader underground at the gold mine at Carrow Creek, about nine hundred metres down. We call the loader a bogger, it's a low, long machine that scoops broken rock out of the stopes, the big holes left after a blast, and carries it to the trucks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the rhythm of a shift like down there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pre-start checks at six, then down the decline, the spiral road, in the light vehicle with my offsider Jono, which is what we call the second person on a crew. I'll bog a stope for most of the shift, and after a blast I sit and wait for the fumes to clear, which is when I eat my sandwiches. The noise and the heat get to you by the end, but I've done it twenty-six years and I still like the feeling of a clean stope floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now, that the technology's useful in places but it isn't magic. We've had a remote-control bogger trial for three years and it still needs someone like me to fix its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can plan to stop at sixty-two like Ruth and I worked out on the kitchen table. Four years, pay off the last bit of the car loan, top up the retirement fund, done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, keep my union membership, and keep using that chatbot thing now and then to sort out letters and pension questions. I might do the remote-loader course anyway if they offered it, because it's easier on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty comfortable. Like a normal week, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Daniel set it up on my phone. I used it to write a complaint to the council about the potholes on Mill Street, and to understand a letter from the pension fund. It's handy, but I check what it says with a person after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, what's the biggest thing that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees and the gold price. If gold drops, they put a mine like ours on care and maintenance, which means shut but not closed. That's happened to me once before, in 2013, and AI had nothing to do with it.

S0.say: I'd say the technology is useful in places but it isn't magic. Our remote-control loader trial has run for three years and still needs someone like me to fix its mistakes.
S0.think: Privately it means I can stop at sixty-two as Ruth and I planned. Four more years, pay off the car, top up the retirement fund, and finish.
S0.do: Keeps working and stays in the union, using a chatbot now and then for letters and pension questions. Would take the remote-loader course if it were offered because it's easier on his back.
S0.quote: If gold drops, they put a mine like ours on care and maintenance, which means shut but not closed.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is calm here and points out that his real everyday risk is the gold price, not AI. He's used a chatbot for practical jobs but double-checks it with a person, which fits his steady streak. He'd take remote training for his body's sake, not his career's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table on how remote operations come in, who gets trained and who doesn't. I'd say it calmly, though, because shouting doesn't help on a Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the boggers go remote first, then the trucks, then the drillers. I'm average at the job, so I won't be first picked, but I'm not last either. I reckon if I get on the training list early, I could finish my four years in a chair on the surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for tele-remote loader training in the first month, which means driving the bogger from a screen up top. I'd ask the union delegate to push for seniority in who gets the seats. And Ruth and I would pay the car loan off early, so we're not carrying anything if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I can see a way through. It's like watching the gauge dip, not the engine stopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jono, my offsider. He's forty and he hates screens worse than I do. And the young ones who came in for the big wages and haven't got a trade behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't stand screens, but you'd go for the screen job. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, you caught me. I don't love it, but I've seen two guys do it on the trial and they still go home tired but not sore. If it's proven, I'll try it, that's always been me.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table on how remote operations come in and who gets trained. I'd say it calmly, because shouting doesn't help on a Monday morning.
S1.think: Privately I think loaders go remote first, then trucks, then drills. If I get on the training list early I could finish my last four years in a chair on the surface.
S1.do: Puts his name down for tele-remote loader training in the first month and asks the union delegate to push for seniority in allocating seats. Pays off the car loan early with his wife so they carry no debt.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but able to see a way through, like a gauge dipping rather than the engine stopping.
S1.quote: It's like watching the gauge dip, not the engine stopping.
S1.fieldNote: Wei treats steady change as a manageable problem, partly because he has watched the remote trial work with his own eyes. He admits a contradiction about screens with good humour. His instinct is both personal (get trained early) and collective (seniority rules through the union).

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments stepping in, fast, with income support for the whole town. And I'd say it at the pub as much as online, because people would be scared and someone has to talk sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, out of work, with a few months saved and two years short of my plan. The remote seat I was counting on, that goes too if the machines can run themselves. That's the bit that gets me, there's no step to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back, no trip to see Anna's new baby interstate, and I'd stash every overtime dollar. I'd go to every union meeting and sign up for any campaign for a payout to older workers. Once it arrives, I'd look for anything with a wage: driving for the shire council, fixing fences, whatever's left that a robot hasn't been sent to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the cage dropping too fast. My stomach goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The cage, that's the lift down the shaft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, the man cage, the lift. When it drops quicker than normal your stomach comes up. That's this one, the whole thing at once with no time to brace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't do the slow thing I'm good at, which is watching, waiting till it's proven and then jumping on. By the time it's proven it's already here. I'd be making big decisions on guesswork, and I hate that.

S2.say: I'd say governments need to step in fast with income support for the whole town. I'd say it at the pub as much as online, because people would be scared and someone has to talk sense.
S2.think: Privately I'd be sixty, out of work and two years short of my plan with only a few months saved. Even the remote seat I was counting on would go if machines can run themselves.
S2.do: Cancels a trip to see his new grandchild and banks every overtime dollar straight away. Joins union campaigns for payouts to older workers and, after it arrives, looks for any paid work such as council driving or fencing.
S2.feel: Like the lift dropping too fast down the shaft, with his stomach in his throat.
S2.quote: By the time it's proven it's already here.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version removes the thing Wei relies on: time to watch something work before he commits. His fear is specific to the loss of the remote-operator step he had planned for. He still wants to be the calm voice at the pub, even while alarmed himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work to get organised now, while there's time to bargain. Online I'd share whatever the union puts out about a transition plan for mining towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three, past my sixty-two plan. So privately I think I'd probably make it, maybe with a year or two less than I hoped. The remote seat would still be useful for three or four of those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still take the tele-remote training this year, and I'd use the chatbot more, honestly, to read up on what's changing. Ruth and I would put an extra two hundred a fortnight into savings and kill the car loan. I'd tell the union I'm willing to go early if there's a package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. It's a deadline, not an ambush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the union got a package together, how early would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it covered me to sixty-two, I'd go at sixty-one without blinking. If it was just a handshake, I'd hang on as long as they'd let me. It depends on the number, like everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel and Anna?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Anna to keep teaching, kids still need a person. Daniel's in computers, so I'd ask him to explain it to me properly. He'd probably say his own job's more at risk than mine, which would be a funny twist.

S3.say: I'd tell people at work to get organised now while there's still time to bargain. Online I'd share what the union puts out about a transition plan for mining towns.
S3.think: Privately I think I'd probably make it to sixty-three with a year or two less than I hoped. The remote seat would still be useful for a few of those years.
S3.do: Takes the tele-remote training this year and uses the chatbot more to read up on changes. Saves an extra two hundred a fortnight, pays off the car loan and tells the union he would go early for a good package.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadier, because it feels like a deadline rather than an ambush.
S3.quote: It's a deadline, not an ambush.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Wei back his preferred way of working: watch, plan, then act. He is more willing to use AI tools here because they help him read up, not because he likes them. His exit decision is openly about the number on the package.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years to do it right, so no excuses for governments or the company. Retraining for the young ones, pensions for the old ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's mostly fine. I'd be sixty-eight, retired for six years by then. My worry is Carrow Creek itself, because the mine is the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, do my four years, and still do the remote training because it's easier on the body. I'd get more involved in the union's town committee, the one that's meant to plan for after the mine. I'd vote for whoever has an actual plan for places like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for me, uneasy for the town. A slow tide, not a wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the town look like in 2036 in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half the houses on Mill Street empty, maybe. Or maybe they turn the old processing shed into something, I don't know. I honestly can't picture it, and nobody's shown me a picture yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year version that would make you change your own retirement plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the retirement fund goes down with the mining shares. If that happened I might work a bit longer, if there's still anything to work at. But no, mostly I'd stick to sixty-two.

S4.say: I'd say we have ten years to do it right, so there are no excuses for governments or the company. Retraining for the young ones and pensions for the old ones.
S4.think: Privately it's mostly fine for me, because I'd be sixty-eight and long retired. My worry is that the mine is the town, and the town might not survive it.
S4.do: Works his last four years and still takes remote training to spare his body. Gets involved in the union's town committee planning for life after the mine and votes for candidates with a real plan for mining towns.
S4.feel: Calm about himself and uneasy for the town, like a slow tide rather than a wave.
S4.quote: I honestly can't picture it, and nobody's shown me a picture yet.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years mostly protects Wei personally, and he shifts his attention to Carrow Creek. He is honest that he can't imagine the town after the mine. His one personal worry is retirement savings tied to mining shares.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a guaranteed income bridge to sixty-two for older workers who lose their jobs, and somebody actually coming to Carrow Creek with a plan, not a brochure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Safety, maybe. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks who fixes a robot nine hundred metres down when it breaks at two in the morning. That used to be someone I knew.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who fixes a robot nine hundred metres down when it breaks at two in the morning.
portrait: Wei Walsh is a 58-year-old underground loader operator at a gold mine in Carrow Creek, twenty-six years in, planning to stop at sixty-two with his wife Ruth. He waits for things to be proven, then commits, and he has already seen a remote-control loader trial work at his mine. He stays calm if AI stalls, uneasy under steady change because he plans to get onto the remote training early, and alarmed if AGI arrives in two years and leaves no step to stand on. With five or ten years he relaxes into bargaining and saving, and his worry moves to whether his mining town survives.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be out of work at sixty with only a few months saved and no time to see what works before acting.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income bridge to sixty-two for older workers who lose their jobs, and a real plan for Carrow Creek rather than a brochure.
